To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the interaction between exercise and cognition is determined by the intensity and duration of exercise, the type of cognitive task performed and the interaction between the catecholaminergic, glucocorticoid and BDNF systems in the brain.

SMD, moderate-intensity exercise increases NE release in the prefrontalcortex, which facilitates all types of cognitive task, whereas long-duration, moderate-intensity and heavy-intensity exercise increases glucocorticoid and 5-hydoxytryptamine concentrations, which further increase NE release, which increases D1-receptor and α1-adrenergic receptor activation, which inhibits central executive function, but facilitates perception/attention and autonomic function.

the catecholamine hypothesis of the exercise-cognition interaction is correct but the brain concentrations of glucorticoids and 2-hydroxytrytamine must also be included and the role of BDNF must be added.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of acute exercise on cognitive function and the role of catecholamines in this interaction.
the interaction between exercise and cognition.

developing an animal model to test the catecholamine hypothesis for the acute, exercise-cognition interaction, which will allow the development of a more comprehensive model of the interaction between exercise, catecholamines glucocorticoids BDNF and the 5-hydroxtryptamine system, in cognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SMD exercise facilitates cognition, but long-duration moderate and heavy exercise impair cognition, due to increased brain concentrations of catecholamines.
the catecholamine hypothesis for the acute cognitive-exercise interaction in humans needs further clarification, particularly in the context of different exercise intensities × durations.

SMD exercise facilitates all tasks via activation of the locus ceruleus and α2A-adrenergic receptors in the pre-frontal cortex, whereas long-duration, moderate and heavy exercise facilitates some tasks via activation of α1-adrenoceptor and β-adrenoceptor-mediated cAMP production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the catecholamine hypothesis is correct for SMD, moderate intensity exercise, which facilitates cognition, but not for long-duration, moderate and heavy exercise, where the facilitatory effects of catecholamines on cognition are counteracted by the inhibitory effects of glucocorticoid, 5-hydrotryptamine and, in long-duration, moderate intensity exercise only, BDNF.
the catecholamine system in humans is more complicated than that of rodents, which may explain the inconsistencies between studies.

the catecholamine hypothesis for the acute, exercise-cognition interaction needs to be modified to include the following: (1) the effects of different exercise intensities × durations, and different exercise modalities on different cognitive tasks, (2) the role of the brain in the exercise-cognition interaction and (3) the role of glucocorticoid and 5-hyroxytryptamine in the exercise-cognitive interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interaction between catecholamines on brain function is complex.
the catecholamine hypothesis fails to adequately explain how exercise affects cognition.

the brain is a very complex and highly adaptive organ that can respond to different exercise intensities and durations by different mechanisms, and this is reflected in the different cognitive tasks that are affected.
